name: Apple cider vinegar

card.summary: Fermented apple juice drunk diluted for fat loss and clear skin; trials are small and major references describe no good evidence for weight loss.
card.aka: ACV, apple cider vinegar with the mother
card.note: Undiluted vinegar and tablets have been linked to tooth enamel and esophageal injury; may interact with insulin and diuretics.

quick.overview:
Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice first into alcohol and then into acetic acid. It is a common kitchen ingredient and has a long folk-medicine history. In looksmaxxing forums it is promoted as a cheap all-round ingredient for fat loss, skin, hair and digestion.

Published reviews summarised by Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe limited or poor-quality evidence for weight loss. Small studies have looked at blood glucose and cholesterol with modest results, and the Mayo Clinic is quoted as saying it is unlikely to cause meaningful weight loss.
quick.mechanism: The active component is generally taken to be acetic acid, about 5 percent of the liquid. Proposed explanations for metabolic effects include slower stomach emptying and effects on post-meal glucose and insulin. Topical claims for acne and dandruff rest on its acidity and in-vitro antimicrobial activity. Which of these mechanisms matter in people has not been established.
quick.risks: Reported problems include tooth enamel erosion, throat or esophageal injury from tablets, reflux and stomach upset, and skin burns or eye injury when used undiluted on the body. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted. Food amounts are generally regarded as safe by regulators; supplements are not regulated as medicines for weight loss.

lead: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) is a vinegar made from apple juice by two-step fermentation: yeast convert sugars to alcohol, then acetic acid bacteria convert the alcohol to acetic acid. The finished product is roughly 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid with almost no fat, protein or micronutrients. Unfiltered versions contain a cloudy cellulose-and-bacteria sediment called the mother. [1][2]

Besides cooking and preserving, ACV is promoted in wellness and looksmaxxing communities as a drink for fat loss and appetite control and as a skin toner, hair rinse and dandruff treatment. Wikipedia states that there is no high-quality clinical evidence that regular consumption helps with weight loss or maintenance, and that major health bodies do not recommend it for therapeutic use. [1] Grokipedia cites the Mayo Clinic as saying it is unlikely to cause meaningful weight loss and cites meta-analyses suggesting modest effects on blood glucose and cholesterol in some trials. [2]

Reviewers who have pooled trials describe small effects for oral use. A 2025 meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials in adults with overweight, obesity or type 2 diabetes reported lower weight, BMI and waist circumference over 4 to 12 weeks, and an umbrella review of 10 meta-analyses reported an average weight change of about 1 kg alongside improvements in several blood-glucose measures. Both sets of authors point to short trials, varied designs and publication bias as limits. [11][12]
Reported adverse effects include dental enamel damage, esophageal injury from tablets, and gastrointestinal discomfort. [1]
infobox: Food; some topical products carry OTC drug labels
Two-step fermentation: yeast make alcohol, Acetobacter make acetic acid. [1]
Bragg (founded 1912), prominent for raw unfiltered ACV from the 1990s per Grokipedia. [2]
Small reductions in weight and post-meal glucose in pooled trials; trials short. [11][12][13]
Low risk if diluted; enamel, throat and skin harms reported. [1]

paras: Apples are washed, crushed and pressed; yeast ferment the juice into cider; acetic acid bacteria then oxidise the alcohol to acetic acid, either added as a culture or as mother vinegar. [1] Per 100 g the product is about 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid, with roughly 22 kcal. [1]
Commercial brands have been reported to vary in acidity, and some were found contaminated with mould and yeast. [1]

Vinegar of various kinds has been used for thousands of years for preservation, food and folk medicine; Grokipedia traces vinegar-based remedies to ancient Babylon, Egypt and Greece and describes apple vinegar becoming a household staple in Europe and colonial America. [2] Wikipedia notes that fruit vinegars became popular in the North Atlantic region in the early 19th century, citing an 1810 cookbook with apple cider vinegar recipes. [1]
Grokipedia describes a rise in health-food marketing after the Second World War and of raw, unpasteurised varieties promoted for their mother in the 1990s. [2]

Wikipedia's article on vinegar traces production to ancient Babylonia around 3000 BCE, describes professional vinegar making in China during the Zhou dynasty, and notes that Orleans became known for a formalised aging process in the late Middle Ages. In 1823 Karl Sebastian Schuzenbach introduced a large-scale industrial process in Baden that shortened fermentation from months to one or two weeks, and later work by Louis Pasteur identified acetic acid bacteria as the fermenting agent. [14]

Grokipedia describes Bragg Live Food Products, founded in 1912, as gaining prominence in the 1990s for raw organic products, which helped establish the cloudy 'with the mother' bottle as the standard wellness form of ACV. [2]

Forum users promote diluted ACV as a face toner, spot treatment, hair rinse and scalp treatment, and as a drink for fat loss. [3] A US-labelled over-the-counter scalp spray containing apple cider vinegar is marketed to help with flaking and itching associated with dandruff, with directions for external use only. [9]
ACV is used in cooking, dressings, marinades and pickling. [2] Wellness sources promote it for digestion and blood sugar control. [2]

Wikipedia reports that there is no high-quality clinical evidence of benefit for weight loss or maintenance and no good evidence that it effectively manages blood glucose or lipids. [1] Grokipedia summarises systematic reviews as finding reductions in post-meal glucose and insulin when taken with carbohydrate meals and modest reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c with use over about eight weeks, while noting that the evidence is limited. [2]

Weight and body composition. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in Nutrients pooled 10 randomised trials in adults with overweight, obesity or type 2 diabetes, using liquid ACV or effervescent tablets, usually with diet or exercise advice, for 4 to 12 weeks. It reported significant reductions in weight, BMI and a small reduction in waist circumference, no significant change in waist-to-hip ratio, and too little data on fat mass to assess it. The authors describe ACV as a possibly useful low-cost adjunct for short-term weight management, and list high heterogeneity, short duration, likely publication bias, mostly high or unclear risk of bias, and one included trial that was later retracted as limitations. [11]

An umbrella review of 10 meta-analyses covering 38 trials reported a pooled weight change of about 1 kg, fasting glucose lower by about 9 mg/dL, postprandial glucose lower by about 15 mg/dL and HbA1c lower by about 0.7 percentage points, with the cholesterol finding rated very low certainty. Its authors describe vinegar as a possible low-cost adjunct for metabolic health while noting high heterogeneity and low quality among several included reviews. [12] A 2025 dose-response meta-analysis of seven trials in 463 adults with type 2 diabetes reported lower fasting glucose and HbA1c, with the HbA1c result rated low certainty. [13]

Appetite and retraction. Grokipedia summarises a 2022 systematic review reporting that vinegar with at least 24.6 mmol of acetic acid suppressed appetite for up to 120 minutes in four of six short-term trials, while 4 to 12 week trials showed no effect on energy intake, and it reports that a 2024 study claiming about 9 percent body-mass loss was retracted by BMJ Group in 2025 over data and methodology concerns. [2]

In laboratory work, a 2018 study reported antimicrobial activity of ACV against Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans in vitro. [4] A 2011 rat study compared apple cider vinegars made with different techniques on blood lipids in animals fed a high-cholesterol diet. [5] Neither study tested skin or weight outcomes in people.

A 2020 systematic review, summarised by Wikipedia, found diluted moderate consumption generally low-risk. Reported harms include esophageal damage from incompletely swallowed tablets, tooth enamel erosion from large amounts, dentin sensitivity, burping, flatulence and more frequent bowel movements. Eye contact may cause corneal injury, and topical use can cause burns. [1]

Wikipedia also lists possible interactions with insulin and diuretics, allergic reactions in people allergic to apples, and a recommendation of caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children. [1] Grokipedia adds that concentrated supplements may worsen reflux and delay stomach emptying. [2]

Grokipedia also reports a 2024 case in which an 84-year-old woman developed acute pancreatitis after taking ACV gummies daily for 30 days, with causality not firmly established, and notes that supplements are not regulated like medicines. Wikipedia separately warns against mixing vinegar with chlorine bleach, which can release chlorine gas. [2][1]

Registered human trials include a comparison of metformin with ACV in people with prediabetes [6], a study of ACV on glycaemic variability and lipids in type 2 diabetes [8], an acute study on an oxidative stress marker after meals in adults with obesity [7], and a study of vinegar and heartburn [10]. Results for these registrations were not available in the listings reviewed. No registered trial listed examines ACV for acne, hair or facial appearance. Meta-analytic findings on glucose and lipids are described above. [2]

On looksmax.org a poster describes ACV as a top ingredient that affects skin, hair, weight, digestion and hormones, listing acne reduction, hair shine and fat burning among its effects. Replies in the thread frame gut health and fermented foods as under-discussed looksmaxxing tools. [3]

The discussion fits a wider pattern in which ACV is positioned as a low-cost staple for leaner bodies, clearer skin and better hair, and it now appears in capsule, gummy and scalp-spray forms as well as the liquid. [3][9][2]

timeline.event: Vinegar use documented in ancient Babylonia, according to Wikipedia's vinegar article. [14]
A British cookbook by Esther Copley includes recipes for apple cider vinegar. [1]
Schuzenbach introduces a large-scale vinegar fermentation process in Baden. [14]
Bragg Live Food Products founded, per Grokipedia. [2]
Raw, unpasteurised ACV with the mother is promoted in wellness circles. [2]
Randomised trial of vinegar with a high-carbohydrate meal reports improved post-meal insulin sensitivity, per Grokipedia. [2]
Laboratory study reports ACV antimicrobial activity in vitro. [4]
A systematic review assesses the safety of vinegar consumption. [1]
Case report of pancreatitis after ACV gummies; a weight-loss study later retracted in 2025. [2]
Meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials reports lower weight, BMI and waist; umbrella review follows. [11][12]

lore.intro: ACV is discussed on looksmax.org as a low-cost generalist tool for skin, hair, fat loss and gut health. [3]

claims.claim: Drinking ACV burns fat and sculpts the body
claims.believers: Proponents say a daily glass of diluted ACV on an empty stomach helps remove excess fat. [3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence for weight loss, and Grokipedia cites the Mayo Clinic as saying meaningful weight loss is unlikely. [1][2]

claims.claim: ACV toner clears acne and balances skin pH
claims.believers: The poster says it kills acne bacteria, reduces oiliness, post-acne marks and blackheads. [3]
claims.experts: A lab study found antimicrobial activity against several microbes in vitro, but no human acne trial is listed. Wikipedia notes topical use can cause burns. [4][1]

claims.claim: ACV rinses improve hair and remove dandruff
claims.believers: Users say a diluted rinse makes hair smooth and shiny and treats dandruff. [3]
claims.experts: A scalp spray containing ACV is sold with an OTC anti-dandruff label, but the label itself does not reference trial data. [9]

claims.claim: Gut health via fermented foods like ACV is a root driver of looks
claims.believers: A reply argues that health equals attractiveness and that gut health is under-researched. [3]
claims.experts: Registered trials examine vinegar on glucose, lipids and heartburn, not appearance. [6][8][10]

claims.claim: ACV helps lose weight and slim the face and waist
claims.believers: Proponents describe a daily diluted drink as helping appetite control and removing excess fat. [3]
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis reported small reductions in weight, BMI and waist over 4 to 12 weeks, with authors citing short trials and bias; Wikipedia states there is no high-quality clinical evidence of benefit. [11][1]

claims.claim: ACV tablets and gummies are a convenient way to get the benefits
claims.believers: Gummies and capsules are marketed as an alternative to drinking the liquid, and they appear in the supplement market alongside the liquid. [2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports esophageal damage from tablets swallowed incompletely, and Grokipedia describes a case report of pancreatitis after gummies with causality not established. [1][2]

angle.goal: Leaner look, clearer skin, healthier hair
chain: Diluted vinegar is drunk with meals or applied diluted to skin and scalp
Claimed: more fullness, steadier blood sugar, less oil and flaking
Possible small drops in weight or waist; cosmetic effects on skin and hair reported by users
angle.text: People drink diluted ACV hoping to eat less and lose a little body fat, which would show as a leaner face and waist, and use diluted rinses and toners on hair and skin. Pooled trials of oral vinegar in adults with excess weight report small reductions in weight and waist measures over weeks, while topical uses rest mainly on acidity and lab antimicrobial findings.
